source_title: My Galaxy phone still can't run Pause Point, so I built my own version with One UI tools
source_excerpt:
If you've ever wondered whether an AI feature on your phone is doing anything useful, Ben Khalesi has probably asked the same question. He has covered AI and Android for Android Police since 2023, with Pixel, Galaxy, Google's apps, and the rest of the Android ecosystem never far behind. Ben is a lifelong geek who trained as an AI engineer and earned a bachelor's in IT, so when the industry announces something new, he's the one who wants to know how everything works behind the scene and what can be trusted.
Pause Point started life as a Google Pixel 11 exclusive, built to catch you mid-doom scroll, but it didn't stick around long.
The Android 17 QPR1 update brought it to Pixels as old as the Pixel 6, and by mid-October 2026 it showed up on a OnePlus 13R running the ColorOS 17 beta.
It looks like Google is pulling the feature away from specific hardware and moving it to the main Digital Wellbeing system system, which would put it on more phones.
Samsung Galaxy owners, though, are still stuck in the waiting room. Until it gets to your phone, you can build a decent stand-in with tools One UI already has.
Pause Point catches your thumb before the feed loads
Most wellbeing tools assume the problem is total screen time. That's fair if you're deliberately binging, but they miss the reflexive opening.
Habitual scrolling rarely starts with a decision. Your hand reaches for the phone, your thumb finds the icon, and the feed is loaded before a conscious thought shows up.
A timer that fires 30 minutes into the session does nothing about that first impulse. Pause Point works because it goes after the impulse.
When you open an app you've marked as distracting, Android 17 stops everything for an unskippable 10 seconds.
During that window, you get options like a short breathing exercise or a nudge toward something healthier, like an audiobook.
Either way, it cuts the urge before the feed ever shows up. The nastiest part (in a good way) is what it takes to quit.
Deactivating Pause Point requires a full device restart, and that's a big hurdle to clear in a weak moment.
No single One UI toggle copies that mix. To get close, I stacked three Samsung features, each covering a different part of what Pause Point does.
Samsung's app timers can lock an app in a minute
The biggest roadblock is Samsung's screen time controls. Go to Settings > Digital Wellbeing and parental controls > App timers .
You'll see a circular graph of your daily screen time, and you can set a custom limit on any app that eats your evenings.
Set the timer to one minute and the app is effectively blocked after you use it.
Its icon turns gray on the home screen, and opening it triggers a pop-up saying the timer has run out.
It's a good baseline, but it runs on the honor system. When the timer runs out, One UI puts a big button right there to add more time or turn the limit off.
You can blow past the block with one mindless tap, which is the kind of tap Pause Point exists to stop.
Without a restart requirement, the timer is a reminder, and it only works if you're disciplined enough to respect it.
Modes lock apps away, but only when you remember to turn them on
For something more aggressive, lock the apps. Samsung keeps two tools under one roof in Settings > Modes and Routines .
On the Modes tab, create a custom Focus or Work mode that restricts specific apps. When the mode is on, those apps are restricted, and their notifications go quiet too .
The catch is that you have to turn on a mode before temptation hits. You can start it manually or tie it to a schedule or location, but either way, you have to predict when you'll get distracted.
One UI's routines react the second you open an app
This is the closest One UI gets to Pause Point
The other tab is the real Pause Point stand-in. Routines are If/Then automations that fire on their own, so they react to what you're doing rather than what you planned.
Go to Settings > Modes and Routines and tap the Routines tab at the bottom of the screen.
Add a new routine. For the "If" condition, choose App opened and pick the apps you open without thinking. That's your tripwire. The "Then" action is the speed bump.
Have the routine switch on system-wide grayscale. In Settings , it's under Accessibility > Vision enhancements .
Now the distracting app opens in black and white. App designers use color on purpose to keep you engaged, and removing bright red badges and flashy buttons breaks the visual reward loop.
You can also set the "Then" action to show a custom notification or trigger Edge lighting. Pick a harsh edge lighting style, and you get a jarring alarm the second the app opens.
One UI's workaround will do until Pause Point shows up
A wall you built yourself comes down a lot easier than one the OS puts up.
Pause Point should eventually show up natively on Galaxy phones and the rest of the Android family. Until it reaches yours, a homemade speed bump is the best you have.
It won't stop a determined scroller, but it beats leaving the road wide open.
